occupations.title: Heating, Air Conditioning, and Refrigeration Mechanics and Installers
electricalKnowledge: Reads wiring diagrams and connects control wiring between thermostat, controls and the equipment
Works at the unit disconnect and the branch circuit that feeds the unit
Tests circuits and components for continuity with a meter
Checks the circuit and protection against the equipment nameplate (minimum circuit ampacity, maximum overcurrent device)
Installs thermostats, timers and low-voltage control wiring
standards: NEC Article 440 (air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment), incl. disconnect within sight of the unit
safetyProcedures: De-energize and lock out at the unit disconnect before opening panels
Verify zero voltage with a meter, including capacitor discharge
Treat low-voltage and line-voltage sections separately
PPE for burns and shock; arc-flash awareness at the supply panel
occupations.verdict: Beginner electrical literacy fits (best in this cluster; real HVAC skill also needs motors, controls, meter testing and LOTO)
occupations.docCodeCorrection: Title in the document ('HVAC Mechanics and Installers') is a short label; the O*NET title is 'Heating, Air Conditioning, and Refrigeration Mechanics and Installers'. SOC code correct.

evidence.says: Tasks include testing circuits for continuity, connecting control wiring per wiring diagrams, installing thermostats; Bright Outlook, 440,900 employed, 40,600 openings
11% growth 2025-35; duties include installing electrical components and wiring; high injury rate incl. burns from electrical parts
Article 440 disconnect must be in sight and readily accessible from the equipment; a panel breaker generally does not serve

headlineChecks.result: Not reproducible. Counting each code once on one basis (O*NET and OOH 2025 employment) gives about 7.3 million for all 23 distinct occupations
headlineChecks.note: Checked on 2026-10-13 against each page; see docs/product/MARKET_FACTS.md. Core six 1,289,200; the 13 adjacent codes with their own figure 5,968,500 (49-2098 is in both groups and counted once; 47-1011.03, 47-2152.04 and 47-4011.01 only repeat a parent's figure; 17-2199.03 shows a larger group's figure). About 78 percent of the adjacent workers are general maintenance workers, construction laborers, construction managers and supervisors, who are not electrical workers. If the 18 rows are summed as listed, with the parents counted again, the adjacent total is 7.80 million.

headlineChecks.claim: ~700K annual openings for the combined 24 occupations
headlineChecks.result: About 616,000, not 700,000, on the same basis (checked 2026-10-13)
headlineChecks.note: Core six 117,200 plus 13 adjacent codes 499,200. 62 percent of the total (385,400) is general maintenance, construction laborers, construction managers and supervisors. The OOH confirms O*NET's openings figure as annual for most codes; for a few the unit is unconfirmed. See docs/product/MARKET_FACTS.md.

headlineChecks.claim: All 18 adjacent occupations are Bright Outlook
headlineChecks.result: False for 5 (confirmed on each O*NET page, 2026-10-13)
headlineChecks.note: Not Bright on their own pages: 47-2211 Sheet Metal Workers, 47-3015 Helpers--Pipelayers/Plumbers, 17-2199.03 Energy Engineers, 47-4011.01 Energy Auditors, 49-2022 Telecom Equipment Installers (declining). The other 13 are Bright (growth for most; 49-9071 for numerous openings; 47-2061 for both). Pages were read through a summarising tool, so spot-check before quoting.

headlineChecks.claim: SOC codes and titles match O*NET
headlineChecks.note: 49-9021 title is Heating, Air Conditioning, and Refrigeration Mechanics and Installers; 49-2095 is Powerhouse, Substation, and Relay repairers, not a power-line installer occupation; the third item in the technology cluster duplicates 49-2098 and the '49-9071?' is wrong; 47-1011 belongs with construction, not technology; 47-2152.04 and 47-1011.03 show parent-group employment and openings, not their own.

headlineChecks.claim: Elevator work fits an NEC app
headlineChecks.note: NEC Article 620 covers the electrical wiring and equipment; ASME A17.1 governs the equipment and its safe maintenance. Flag as a poor fit for a pure NEC app.

doubts: The fetch tool returns summaries from a small model; Bright Outlook, growth and openings values were not read verbatim from the pages. Re-verify any number before it goes in the final document.

BLS OOH pages for sheet metal workers, elevator installers, construction supervisors, telecom installers and security and fire alarm installers returned 403, so BLS figures for those come from O*NET (which uses BLS projections) only.
The Energy Engineers and Energy Auditors counts on O*NET (166,700 and 153,900) look like parent-group figures; Energy Auditors equals the BLS Construction and Building Inspectors figure exactly.
NEC 90.2(B) exclusions (ships, rail rolling stock, aircraft, automobiles, utility generation and substations) were stated from knowledge, not from a page I opened; confirm against the code text.
NFPA 70E page, ASME A17.1 page, OSHA wind and solar pages did not load; the standards for wind, solar and elevators lean on search-result articles and O*NET. OSHA 1910.147, .332 and .333 were opened.
1910.147 itself excludes electrical-utilization installations (covered by 1910.333), so 'LOTO' for electrical workers is really 1910.333 plus NFPA 70E.
The skill mapping to the app's 13 skills is my judgement; I did not inspect the app's skill definitions.
The document says 24 occupations but lists 18 adjacent entries; the other six (core) were not part of this check.
Standards listed without an opened source (UL, TIA, SMACNA, ASHRAE, IEEE, GWO, 1910.268, 1910.269, 1926 Subpart K, EPA 608) come from general knowledge.
